topic.title: the gift in the box
topic.claim: Your parents keep the gift from your first salary in its box. It's the receipt that you turned out okay.
topic.moment: Years later the watch or the saree is still boxed in the cupboard, taken out to show relatives, never worn.

turn.believed: They're saving it for a special occasion that never seems to come.
turn.actually: The gift isn't meant to be used. It's proof the kid they raised made it, kept safe.

topic.because: Using it would wear it out. As an object it's a thing; as a sealed box it's evidence of the day their investment paid back. They're keeping the proof, not the present.
topic.payoff: They never wore it because it was never a gift. It was the receipt that you turned out okay.
topic.feeling: the lump in your throat at being someone's proof
topic.villain: the arrangement that turns a parent's whole effort into one unopened box
topic.behaviour: parents preserve first-salary gifts unused, display them to visitors
topic.mechanism: worn out it's just an object, but kept sealed it's evidence their child made it, so they save it as proof not as a present
topic.group: adults who gave their parents something from their first paycheck
topic.send_to: a friend who still remembers what they bought with their first salary
topic.why_now: year-end, when people look back on how far they've come

cover.headline: Your first-salary gift to your parents is [still in its box]
cover.sub: And they have no plans to take it out.

paragraphs: Your first-salary gift to your parents is still in its box. It will never leave.
slides.why_swipe: Why would anyone keep a gift sealed for years?

paragraphs: If you bought them a phone, it got used every single day until the screen cracked and the battery died by lunch. The watch or the saree is another matter.
The watch still has the plastic on its strap. The saree still smells of the shop, folded in tissue paper that crackles. Years later. Untouched.
slides.why_swipe: If it's hidden away, when does it ever come out?

paragraphs: It comes out when relatives visit. "Beta ne pehli salary se liya tha."
The box goes around the room, from one aunt's hands to the next, and everyone admires it. Then it goes back. Nobody has ever seen it on a wrist.
slides.why_swipe: Why show it off but never wear it?

paragraphs: We assume they're saving it for a special day, a wedding or a puja that finally feels good enough.
That day keeps not coming. It already came, the month your first salary hit your account.
slides.why_swipe: So why does wearing it now feel wrong?

paragraphs: Worn every day, a watch gets scratched and a saree fades, until it's just one more thing in the house.
A boxed one stays that first month. The month you started paying them back.
They ran the same cracked phone for years so your coaching fees, hostel rent and exam forms went through on time.
That box is the first thing that came back.
slides.why_swipe: So what happens when you buy them something better?

paragraphs: Buy them a better watch now and it's on their wrist by Sunday. Suggest the old one gets worn, and you hear "purana wala theek hai jahan hai."
The new one is a gift. The old one is the verdict.
You think you gave them a watch.
They kept the receipt that you turned out okay.

end.save: Come back to it the next time you're home and the box comes out for a relative.
end.send: Send to the friend who still remembers exactly what they bought with their first salary.
end.promise: The money and feelings Indian families never name.

draft.caption: What did you buy your parents with your first salary, and is it still in the box?
draft.alt_text: A nine-slide text carousel. It argues that Indian parents keep the watch or saree their child bought with their first salary sealed in its box, plastic still on the strap, and bring it out only to show relatives. A phone gets used till it cracks, and a newer watch gets worn, but the first one stays boxed because it marks the month the child started paying them back after years of sacrifice, like running the same cracked phone so coaching fees and hostel rent got paid. It ends: you think you gave them a watch; they kept the receipt that you turned out okay.
